speaker: Moses Kagan
title: Repositioning 80 Apartment Buildings with Moses Kagan
question: In multifamily value-add real estate development, why do high-volume sponsors often avoid acting as their own in-house general contractor on heavy renovation projects?
guest: We don't GC ourselves. In the beginning I thought we might, and my partner got his contractor's license for that reason. It turns out that's not a great model for us, in part because we want to do a lot of projects at once, and no GC is going to oversee 10 or 20 individual rehab projects—it's just not feasible, so we were going to be forced to use third-party GCs anyway. Also, GCing your own deals creates weird incentive misalignment. A contractor, almost by definition, is trying to do as little work as they can for whatever they're getting paid, while the investors in a building want the most work they can get for the money. We have found it is better to set ourselves up as 100% pure advocates for the investors, who are our partners, and maintain true arm's-length relationships with the contractors. We have very close repeat relationships—one guy has done around 40 buildings for us since 2009, and two others have done north of 15 each. On our side, we oversee design, handle materials purchasing, and hire and oversee the contractors, but we are not ourselves the contractors.

points.core: No single general contractor can feasibly oversee ten to twenty simultaneous rehabs.
points.note: Accept: span-of-control ceiling where running many concurrent renovation sites forces reliance on multiple third-party GCs anyway. Do not credit: generic claims that construction is 'hard to manage' without tying to multi-project concurrency limits.

points.core: Contractors face a structural incentive to minimize work performed for a fixed fee.
points.note: Accept: principal-agent conflict where GCs profit by doing less scope/cost for the contract price while building owners/investors want maximum work per dollar. Do not credit: generic distrust of contractors or vague mentions of 'conflicts of interest' without explaining the economic trade-off.

points.core: Arm's-length contracting keeps sponsors aligned as pure advocates for their building investors.
points.note: Accept: separating the sponsor from the GC role preserves fiduciary alignment and tough oversight on behalf of LPs/partners. Do not credit: generic advice to 'hire good contractors' or both-sides hedging claiming in-house GCing is equally aligned.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
High-volume sponsors usually avoid self-performing as general contractor on heavy renovations because it concentrates risk and distracts from their core business, and the margin saved rarely compensates.

The main reason is risk transfer. A third-party GC working under a fixed-price or guaranteed-maximum contract absorbs cost overruns, schedule delays, subcontractor defaults, worker injuries and construction-defect claims. An in-house GC puts all of that liability, plus licensing, bonding, insurance and workers' compensation exposure, on the sponsor's own balance sheet.

Lenders and investors also prefer an arm's-length contractor. Related-party construction fees create a conflict of interest, invite scrutiny over whether pricing is at market, and can complicate loan draws and completion guarantees.

There is also an operational problem. Heavy rehab (structural, mechanical, plumbing and electrical systems, permits) requires specialized supervision, subcontractor relationships and a standing payroll. That overhead is hard to keep fully used when deal flow is lumpy and spread across markets, whereas local GCs bring established subcontractor pricing and permitting knowledge.

Sponsors therefore tend to keep construction management oversight in-house and outsource execution, reserving self-performance for light, repetitive interior unit turns.

points.why: The candidate discusses difficulty keeping crews utilized across uneven deal flow and multiple markets without identifying a limit on how many simultaneous rehabs one GC can oversee.
The candidate frames fixed-price contracts as risk transfer and leaves out the contractor’s incentive to minimize work while investors seek the most work for their money.
The candidate ties arm’s-length contracting to market pricing and financing scrutiny without explaining how separating the roles lets sponsors oversee contractors solely on investors’ behalf.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
High-volume multifamily sponsors typically outsource heavy renovations to third-party general contractors to transfer risk, preserve geographic agility, and satisfy institutional capital partners. Heavy value-add scopes—such as structural repairs, major mechanical upgrades, and building-envelope replacements—carry substantial cost-overrun, safety, and construction-defect liabilities. Engaging an external contractor under a fixed-price or guaranteed maximum price contract shifts execution risk away from the sponsor while avoiding burdensome multi-state licensing, bonding, and insurance requirements.

Building an in-house construction arm also introduces high fixed payroll overhead that becomes a drag whenever acquisition volume slows. Moreover, high-volume sponsors invest across multiple metros where established local contractors command stronger subcontractor relationships, permitting familiarity, and pricing leverage than an out-of-market team can easily replicate. Finally, institutional limited partners and bridge lenders closely scrutinize affiliate contractors for conflicts of interest around fee double-dipping and change orders, leaving sponsors better served focusing on higher-margin acquisitions, capital raising, and asset management.

points.why: The response cites geographic reach and payroll overhead but never explains how simultaneous rehabs exceed a single GC’s supervisory capacity.
The response discusses risk transfer under fixed-price contracts without explaining the contractor’s incentive to minimize work at the agreed price.
The response mentions scrutiny of affiliate fees and change orders without explaining how arm’s-length contracting lets the sponsor oversee the GC solely on investors’ behalf.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
High-volume sponsors usually avoid being their own general contractor on heavy renovations because it keeps risk and responsibility with someone else. A third-party GC working under a fixed-price or guaranteed-maximum-price contract, often backed by payment and performance bonds, carries much of the cost-overrun and schedule risk. That matters on gut rehabs, where hidden structural, plumbing, electrical and HVAC problems and permitting delays are common. An in-house GC leaves all of that on the sponsor's balance sheet and on investors' returns.

Governance is the second reason. Lenders and limited partners tend to distrust self-dealing, because a sponsor that pays its own construction fees and approves its own change orders and draw requests has no independent check. Many capital partners want an outside contractor whose work is independently inspected.

Third, a construction company is a separate business with its own licensing in each state, insurance, defect and injury liability, and permanent staff. Deal flow is uneven, so that fixed overhead becomes a burden when acquisitions slow. Established GCs also have better access to subcontractors, buying power and skills in specialized trades. Sponsors therefore stick to what they do best, which is finding and financing deals and managing the assets. Some do keep in-house teams for light interior unit turns.

The response uses fixed pricing to explain risk transfer and omits the contractor’s incentive to minimize work for the agreed price while investors seek more work per dollar.
The response explains how separating the sponsor and contractor roles preserves independent oversight of construction spending and work on behalf of investors.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
High-volume multifamily value-add sponsors often avoid acting as their own general contractor on heavy renovations primarily to transfer construction risk and preserve scalability. Heavy rehabs involving structural, mechanical, electrical, or plumbing systems carry substantial exposure to hidden defects, permitting delays, and cost overruns. Hiring an independent third-party GC allows sponsors to shift much of that risk through guaranteed maximum price (GMP) contracts, performance bonds, and third-party warranties, whereas an in-house GC leaves every overrun and liability on the sponsor’s own balance sheet.

Institutional lenders and joint-venture equity partners also frequently prefer or require a seasoned, bonded third-party GC with independent balance-sheet capacity, and they scrutinize in-house contracting for potential fee-stacking and conflicts of interest. Finally, heavy construction demands significant fixed overhead—such as estimators, licensed superintendents, insurance, and local subcontractor networks—that is difficult to scale across multiple markets and fluctuating deal pipelines. By outsourcing execution to specialized local GCs, high-volume sponsors stay lean and focus their capital and talent on acquisitions, financing, and asset management.

points.why: The response discusses scaling overhead across markets and fluctuating deal pipelines but does not identify the limit on how many simultaneous rehabs one GC can oversee.
The response mentions fee-stacking and conflicts of interest without explaining the contractor’s incentive to minimize work for a fixed price while investors seek the most work per dollar.
The response frames third-party contracting as risk transfer and a financing preference without explaining how separating the roles preserves the sponsor’s ability to advocate for investors.

High-volume multifamily sponsors often hire a third-party general contractor for heavy renovations because running a construction company requires a different team and puts more of the execution risk on the sponsor. Structural work and major building-system upgrades require dedicated superintendents, licensed trades, permitting, safety oversight, and close coordination, especially when residents remain on site. Even a sponsor with a large portfolio may have uneven workloads across markets, making it expensive to keep those teams staffed between projects.

An established GC brings local subcontractor relationships and takes contractual responsibility for coordinating the work, meeting schedule commitments, and correcting defects. A well-scoped fixed-price or guaranteed-maximum-price contract can also shift some cost-overrun risk to the GC, though unforeseen conditions and scope changes can still fall to the owner. The sponsor keeps control of the renovation scope and budget while its team focuses on financing, asset management, and leasing.

points.why: The response describes uneven workloads between projects and omits the limit on how many simultaneous rehabs one GC can oversee.
The response discusses shifting cost-overrun risk but does not explain the GC’s incentive to minimize work for a fixed price while investors seek the most work per dollar.
The response says the sponsor retains control of scope and budget but does not connect arm’s-length contracting to the sponsor’s ability to advocate solely for investors.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
For high-volume sponsors, the constraint is often management capacity. A heavy renovation, especially in an occupied building, requires someone on site to sequence trades, coordinate access with property managers, and resolve surprises as walls come down. Acting as the general contractor may save the contractor’s fee, but it also means staffing and supervising that work across several properties at once. Delayed unit turnovers can erase the savings through lost rent and added carrying costs.

An experienced third-party GC brings field supervision and subcontractor relationships, takes contractual responsibility for construction quality and scheduling, and can assume some cost-overrun risk, depending on the contract. The sponsor still oversees the budget and bears the financial impact of delays, but its team has more time to acquire, finance, and manage projects across the portfolio.

points.why: The response describes the staffing burden of concurrent rehabs but stops short of saying the workload exceeds what one GC can feasibly oversee.
The response discusses fees and cost-overrun risk without explaining how a fixed price rewards the GC for doing less while investors want more work per dollar.
The response frames outsourcing as a way to free sponsor capacity and omits how arm’s-length contracting preserves the sponsor’s role as an advocate for investors.
